rent-leaves-room.title: Rent that leaves enough for everything else
rent-leaves-room.line: After I pay rent each month, there's still enough for groceries, bills, and a little put away.
rent-leaves-room.writerNotes: The core end state: housing stops eating the rest of the budget. Why test: why want this? To have money for the rest of life, which is the end, not a step inside this pain. Swap test: the title and line name rent, so it doesn't fit Broke or No savings unchanged. Distinct from fair-rent (fairness of the price, not the share of pay).

predictable-rent.title: Knowing what my rent will be next year
predictable-rent.line: When my lease comes up for renewal, I already know about what next year's rent will be, and I know I can pay it.
predictable-rent.writerNotes: End state is certainty about future housing cost, the thing renters dread at renewal. Why test: why want it? To plan the year without fear, which is the end itself; a rent cap or longer lease would be the fix. Swap test: lease renewal ties it to this pain. Distinct from staying-put (staying in place) because this is about the number, not the address.

staying-put.title: Staying in my home as long as I want
staying-put.line: I can keep living in the home and neighborhood I know for years, without a rent increase pushing me out.
staying-put.writerNotes: End state is not being priced out of one's own home. Why test: why want it? Because it's home: school, friends, routine; that's the end. Swap test: Eviction is about a legal process and Gentrification about neighbors; this one is about my rent pushing me out. Flagged against predictable-rent and near-what-matters.

room-for-family.title: Affording enough room for my family
room-for-family.line: We can afford a place where the kids have a bedroom and nobody sleeps on the couch, and we still cover our other bills.
room-for-family.writerNotes: High rent often means paying a lot for too little space. Why test: why want more room? So the family lives comfortably; that's the end. Swap test: Bad housing is about the place being run-down; this names the rent-for-space tradeoff. Flagged against own-place.

own-place.title: Affording a place of my own
own-place.line: I can pay the rent on a place by myself, without needing roommates to cover it.
own-place.writerNotes: For single renters, high rent means roommates they didn't choose. Why test: why want it? Privacy and control over home life, the end itself. Swap test: Living with parents is about not having moved out; this is about affording to live alone. Flagged against room-for-family, since both are about what kind of place the rent lets me have.

near-what-matters.title: Affording to live near my work and family
near-what-matters.line: I can pay the rent on a place close to my job and the people I love, so I'm not trading cheaper rent for an hour on the road each way.
near-what-matters.writerNotes: High rent pushes people far out. Why test: why want to live close? Time and closeness to people, which are ends. Swap test: Commute is about lost hours; this is about rent forcing the tradeoff, so it names the cost. Flagged against staying-put.

fair-rent.title: Paying a fair rent for the place I get
fair-rent.line: My rent matches what my place is really worth, and no hidden fees get added on top.
fair-rent.writerNotes: End state is not being overcharged. Why test: why want a fair rent? Partly to pay less (rent-leaves-room), but feeling not taken advantage of is its own end; a renter can afford rent and still be overcharged. Swap test: rent and fees tie it here. Flagged against rent-leaves-room.

rent-builds-something.title: Housing payments that build something for me
rent-builds-something.line: Part of what I pay for housing each month adds up to savings or a share in my home, instead of just disappearing.
rent-builds-something.writerNotes: End state is that the biggest monthly bill leaves something behind. Why test: why want it? Long-term security from money already spent; the end, not a step. Swap test: Buying a home is about owning outright; this applies to renters too (shared-equity, savings). Closest cross-pain risk is Buying a home, which the screen should try.

town-affordable.title: Rents in my town that ordinary paychecks can cover
town-affordable.line: Teachers, cooks, nurses, and people with jobs like mine can all afford to rent in my town.
town-affordable.writerNotes: The shared version: rent is set by the local market, so this pain is partly about the world, which allows one world-level dream. Why test: why want it? So I and people like me can live here, the end. Swap test: Gentrification is about longtime neighbors being priced out of a changing area; this is about rents matching local wages anywhere. Distinct from rent-leaves-room because it's about everyone, not my budget.

overlaps.reason: Both protect against rent increases, one as a known number and one as not being pushed out.
Both are about where I can afford to live, one about staying and one about being close to work and family.
Both are about what kind of place the rent lets me have, more space for a family or a place without roommates.
A fair rent may read as a way to rent that leaves enough for everything else.
